en: The Root Treatise on the Gate of Right Reasoning in the Science of Logic (Hetuvidyānyāyamukha-śāstra),
composed by Bodhisattva Mahāvyutpatti,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Desiring to distinguish and uphold the reality within the meanings of proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), I have composed this treatise.
The collection of statements such as the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) constitutes the proof; herein, it is merely according to one's own intention.
That which is stated for the sake of what is to be established is called the "thesis," and it cannot be set aside by a meaning contrary to its characteristics.

Regarding the phrase "the thesis and so forth are the proof through multiple statements": because the meaning is not yet understood by the opponent through the verbal exposition of multiple statements—namely the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*udāharaṇa*)—these multiple statements are termed "proof" (*sādhana*) in works such as the *Vādanyāya*.

Furthermore, the statement that "a single member [of the proof] suffices" is intended to demonstrate that the nature of being a valid proof (*sādhana*) is established as a whole; from this, one should understand that the failure of any constituent part constitutes a fault of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*).
The term "in this" (*asmin*) signifies either the commencement of the treatise or the sense of selection and retention; it is called "in this" because it refers to the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
The term "only" (*eva*) has the sense of exclusion or specification.
"According to one's own intention" (svābhiprāya) indicates that one disregards the tenets of formal treatises and establishes [a position] according to one's own inclination.
"Desire" (ruci) is what is to be established; that is, the lack of desire serves as the nature of the means of establishment.
If it were otherwise, then the probandum (*sādhya*), as well as fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), would also have to be called the thesis (*pakṣa*).
To clarify that the thesis is free from other such faults, it is said: "It cannot be set aside by a meaning contrary to its own characteristics."
If it is not refuted by a statement whose meaning is contradictory, such as the proposition "all statements are false";
or if it does not contradict the previously established tenet, such as the son of a *śṛgāla* (a fox) establishing that "sound is eternal";

or if, because it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), there is no inference (*anumāna*) available to refute it by means of a contradiction with a commonly accepted statement, such as saying "the hare-holder [is not the moon], because the moon does not exist."

Furthermore, regarding an existent phenomenon (*dharma*), there is the refutation of a meaning that contradicts what has been established as being in conflict with either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), such as when one attempts to establish that "sound is not audible" or "a jar is permanent."

Regarding those who claim that when the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) contradict each other, it is called a "contradiction of the thesis" (*pakṣavirodha*), this is not a fault of the thesis;

for in this case, the statement "Sound is permanent because everything is impermanent" is a faulty formulation of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) as a methodological device, which, by means of the application of the example, demonstrates that [the subject] is not included among "everything."
This reason does not exist, because sound is included within "all";
or, because it constitutes a part of the very thesis to be established, this meaning is unestablished, which is termed a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

The analogy also contains a fault, because it first demonstrates the absence of the thesis through a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), and only subsequently states the absence of the reason.
It should have been stated thus:
"All things are impermanent," because this expresses the meaning of "not non-all."
However, since this inverted statement claims that "all things are impermanent," the analogy used here is also flawed.
Thus, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the fallacious thesis (*pratipakṣa*) have been explained.
Since the reason (*hetu*) and the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are for the most part properties of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), their specific characteristics shall now be demonstrated.
The logical reason (hetu) is established with respect to the similar class (sapakṣa) as being present, absent, or both;
with respect to each of the dissimilar classes (vipakṣa), it is likewise threefold: present, absent, or both.
Is it not the case that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is generally defined as the synthesis of the property to be established (*sādhya*) with the locus?
Why, then, is it said here that the thesis refers exclusively to the factual base (*dharmin*)?
There is no fault in this.
Because the term "thesis" (*pakṣa*) is also applied to its specific components, as in the expression "burning the robe";
however, there are some schools for whom the term "thesis" refers exclusively to the property (*dharma*).
Herein, the "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*) is taken to mean that which is definitively and mutually accepted by both the proponent and the opponent.
The same applies to existence, non-existence, and so forth within the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

Why is this? Because here we rely solely on the cause of realization (*pramāṇa*); it is merely through the power of cognition that the meaning of what is taught is understood, unlike a generative cause (*janaka-hetu*), which functions by producing an effect.
If that were so, since cognition would already have been taken as the cause of comprehension (*pariccheda-hetu*), this statement would lose its capacity to establish the thesis.

This is not the case; rather, it serves to cause the opponent to recollect what was previously established for them. Therefore, in this context, it is rightly said that one takes only that which is accepted by both parties as certain.

Therefore, if there is a disagreement between the proponent and the opponent regarding a particular point, that point certainly cannot be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), as in the case of attempting to prove: "Sound is impermanent, because it is visible by the eye."
Furthermore, if the opponent does not grant the same admission, it is like the case of the *Prakaṭārthavādin* regarding the reason "because of being a product" (*kṛtakatvāt*).

Or, if there is doubt, it is like when one gives rise to uncertainty based on smoke and so forth, establishing that "fire exists as a combination of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), because smoke is presently perceived."
Alternatively, in some cases, a thesis is not established; for example, the attempt to establish that "the self is omnipresent because pleasure and so forth arise in all places.
All such statements of every variety mentioned above are incapable of proving the point.
The same should be stated accordingly regarding its presence or absence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and so forth.

Among the reasons that will be explained as contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), only those expressed with words that are universally accepted and definitive are designated as "proof" (*sādhana*) or "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*).
This is not a case of mutual non-establishment or of words of hesitation, for it must further depend upon establishment.
Now, when establishing a thesis (*pakṣadharma*), one should logically establish that property by means of another property as the reason (*hetu*):

whether to establish that the subject (*dharmin*) exists, or to establish it as non-existent. For example, one might establish that "the *paramātman* exists, because we perceive distinct individual things possessing a common universal."
Alternatively, it may be established as "non-existent, because it cannot be apprehended.
What is the meaning of this?
Here, one merely establishes the thesis that "a distinct entity necessarily has a single cause," rather than establishing "supremacy"; therefore, this fault does not apply.
If it is established as "non-existent," one likewise provisionally designates it as a "non-apprehendable phenomenon"; therefore, there is no fault of it being an existent phenomenon.

If one were to establish another existent phenomenon by means of an existent phenomenon, or establish its property [by means of it], such as establishing fire by means of smoke, or establishing tangibility by means of fire—what would the meaning of this be?
In this context, it is not the case that "fire" and "touch" are established as the thesis (*pakṣa*); rather, it is these associated entities that are being established.
Otherwise, if fire were established based on smoke and touch were established based on fire, it would follow that a portion of the thesis itself would function as the reason (*hetu*).
Furthermore, within this context, it is not intended to establish the existence of fire or touch, as their existence is already commonly known.

Moreover, since here one examines that which is to be established, the property (dharma) and the locus of the property (dharmin) are posited, rather than the quality (guṇa) and the possessor of the quality (guṇin); therefore, there is no fault.
Re-stated in verse:
There is no existent that is established by means of an existent, nor is there an existent established by means of a phenomenon;
rather, it is by means of a phenomenon that its corresponding phenomenon is established—thus is an existent established.

If one establishes the thesis: "Sound is not eternal, because karma and so forth would have to be eternal, and that which is eternal should be perceivable," how is this called the *pakṣadharma* (the property of the subject)?

This explains that fault through the categories of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*); because there is something to be established, the word "should" (*syāt*) is employed, and since he first established "permanent, because it is formless," he subsequently establishes only the thesis to refute the fault of that reason.
If one establishes the proposition in this way: "Sound is impermanent, because that which is produced is non-eternal, and that which is eternal is not produced," how is this further characterized?
It is a method of illustration (*dṛṣṭāntopāya*).

The similar instance (*sādharmya*) and the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*) explain their respective reasons in due order, because the thesis (*pakṣa*) necessarily follows [the reason], and because where there is no thesis, there is necessarily no reason.

In this context, by means of the application (*upanaya*), the reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is demonstrated: thus, this sound is necessarily produced and not unproduced; this state of being produced is necessarily a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
To state it again in verse:
"The reason follows the thesis;
where there is no thesis, the reason does not exist."
Relying on the fifth illustration, one knows the reason through its application;

by this, the method of refutation through counter-argument is already explained. Since "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is observed in the impermanent and not observed in the permanent, it is thus established that "sound is not permanent, because it would otherwise not be produced."
Therefore, the methods of conforming to establish [a position] and opposing to refute it are not separate reasons for interpretation.
As I have already extensively analyzed in my refutation of the Sāṃkhya school, I shall now cease this extensive debate on ancillary arguments.
Thus, there are three distinctions in the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*):
namely, its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), its absence from them, and both.
First, the word "and" (*ca*) is excluded.

In this context, if a category is proximate and equivalent to the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*), it is called the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*), because all objects are termed "categories.
If the property to be established is absent, it is called the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*); this does not mean it is either contradictory to or different from the similar instance.
If they were contradictory, there would need to be a specific distinction made;
if they were different, there would be no cause [for their coexistence].
By this principle, "the state of being produced" can establish both "impermanence" and "selflessness," as they are not contradictory.
If a property can establish a contradictory thesis, it is the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*), which is termed a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*).
Just as with the non-contradictory (*aviruddha*), so too is the contradictory:
because where the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is absent, [the reason] is necessarily absent.
It is not like the case of a jar and so forth, where doubt arises because an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not exist between them.

This is because the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is observed to exist in things such as cloth even apart from jars, whereas this reason [of being produced] does not exist apart from impermanence in things such as the non-self (*anātman*).
How can a distinct phenomenon (dharma) function in a distinct location?
Because they are similar, it is not stated by a different name that "this is precisely that," and thus there is no fault.
If it is not stated as something distinct, how can this reason be called the "property of the subject" (pakṣadharma)?
In this context, it is stated that [the reason] must necessarily be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), but it is not intended to say that it is *only* a property of the subject.
If that were so, would the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) also be called the subject? No;
for it is stated elsewhere that [the subject] is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
The reason must be without exception for an inference (*anumāna*) to be established; therefore, they are not similar.

Furthermore, each of these possesses three types: namely, [the reason] being present in all similar instances (*sapakṣa*), while regarding the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), it may be present, absent, or both present and absent.
Regarding their absence from the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and their presence therein, there are likewise three such distinctions for each.

If the thesis of impermanence were entirely devoid of a dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), as in the case of those who do not posit the existence of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, how could it be said that [the reason] is absent in that place?
If that [reason] does not exist in that [subject], it does not occur there, and thus there is no doubt whatsoever; therefore, this fault does not arise.

In this way, nine types of *pakṣadharma* (probandum-property) are formed; their characteristics will be briefly explained in their respective order. For example: one might establish "Sound is eternal, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*)," or one might establish "It is impermanent, because it is produced (*kṛtakatva*)."
Some establish [the thesis] as "it is impermanent because it is produced by uninterrupted effort";
some establish it as "it is permanent because it is a product";
or some establish it as "it is permanent because it is audible."
Some establish [the subject] as "permanent," because it is produced by uninterrupted effort;
some [establish it] as "not produced by uninterrupted effort," because it is impermanent;
others establish it as "impermanent," because it is produced by uninterrupted effort.
Or it is established as "permanent, because it is not subject to contact.
These nine types are subsumed within two verses:
Permanent, impermanent, and produced by effort; Constant, abiding, and the nature of solidity.
Not effort, not transition, and not change— these arise from the nine beginning with the "object of cognition" (*prameya*).
The object of cognition, activity, impermanence, the nature of activity,
hearing, vigor, impermanence, vigor, and lack of tangibility— these depend on the nine beginning with "permanence" (*nitya*).
Thus, these are explained through their distinctions as the "similar" (*sapakṣa*), the "contradictory" (*viruddha*), and the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, the root verse says:
"In the presence of the similar class and both [classes], and its absence in the dissimilar class—this is the 'similar' reason.
That which is the reverse of this is the 'contradictory. All others are 'inconclusive.'"
In this context, there are only two types of reasons: those that are present in all similar instances (sapakṣa) and entirely absent from dissimilar instances (vipakṣa);
and those that are either present or absent in some similar instances, while being entirely absent from dissimilar instances.
From each of the first and last [groups] of three, one takes the middle one.
Furthermore, only two types are said to be contradictory because they can establish perversion: namely, that which exists in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) and both types;
and that which is entirely absent from the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Among the second triad, one takes the first and the last two.
As for the remaining five types, both their causes and their contradictions are indeterminate; this is the meaning of being a "cause of doubt" (*saṃśaya-hetu*).

Furthermore, regarding all characteristics of reasons (*hetu*) and so forth, it is stated that the subject and the predicate share the same number and belong to the same class. This is to prevent the claim that two contradictory characteristics might coexist in a single locus and still function as a reason, or that a characteristic might fail to be a pervading reason (*avyāpaka-hetu*) because it performs the same function within a single class.

Logically, all four types should be called "inconclusive reasons" (*anaikāntika-hetu*), because both [the presence of the reason in the subject and its absence from the dissimilar instances] apply to them.
What is meant by "that which is heard"?
It is due to its being unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
Because those specific differences among the properties to be established that are not shared [with the dissimilar class] encompass all such cases, they are all causes of doubt;
for they are exclusively excluded from that which possesses the property [of the similar class] while being included within it.
All existing things are common [to all], for there is no cause for distinction.
This [commonality] is merely non-contradictory with respect to them; it is the nature of a cause for doubt.
If, within that [context], both parts are present, this is also a definitive cause, because it distinguishes [the subject] from others; this is called "differentiation" (viśeṣa).
If one were to admit that the nature of sound is eternal, this [reason] would constitute a valid probans (*sādhana*).
If, at that time, there were no demonstration of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth as a reason for impermanence, such a case might be possible;
however, since it is impossible for two mutually contradictory properties to be perceived simultaneously in a single object, this is a reason of doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*).
Furthermore, within this context, the power of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scriptural authority (*āgama*) is superior; therefore, one should rely upon these to seek certainty.
The preceding verse summarizes:
"If a phenomenon is unique, common, or characterized by contradiction,"
In all such cases, these are of the nature of causes for doubt. Whether it be a pseudo-probans (*asiddha*) regarding the property (*dharma*),
the locus (*dharmin*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*), or a specific attribute (*viśeṣa*),
these constitute contradictory reasons (*viruddhahetu*), provided there is no sublation (*bādhā*).
When examining the fundamental tenets of a school through critical investigation, if what is asserted is contradictory or harmful, it results in hesitation and error;
other than this, there is no such thing as a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Thus have the reasons and pseudo-reasons been explained.
I shall now explain the simile and the fallacious simile:
when the reason is stated, it must follow from the thesis;
if the thesis is absent, the reason does not exist.
These two are called analogies; all others are similar to these. There are two kinds of analogies:
those based on similarity (sādharmya) and those based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya).
A "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) refers to establishing: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced by uninterrupted effort;
for all things produced by uninterrupted effort are seen to be impermanent, just like a jar and so forth."
Regarding "dissimilar properties" (*vaidharmya*): it refers to the statement, "Whatever is permanent is not produced by non-intermittent effort, such as space.

The former [the similar property] is both a negation and an affirmation, while the latter merely precludes confusion; this is because the meaning is inferred through the methods of joint presence (*anvaya*) and joint absence (*vyatireka*).

Therefore, although one does not establish the actual existence of such things as "great empty space" (*mahākāśa*) through formal debate, it is nonetheless possible to demonstrate that the thesis is non-existent and that the meaning of the absence of a reason is established.

Furthermore, for what reason is it said in the first case that the reason follows upon the thesis, while in the second case it is said that the thesis does not exist because the reason is absent, rather than saying that the thesis does not exist because the reason is absent?

By stating it in this way, one demonstrates that the reason is definitely present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and entirely absent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), rather than stating it erroneously.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"One should prove its permanence by means of its non-being produced, Or establish what is produced by means of its impermanence."
If that were so, it would result in what was not stated: namely, non-pervasiveness and the lack of conjunction with pleasure and so forth, as well as their separation.
Thus have the two sets of concordant and discordant analogies regarding the conjunction and separation of these two factors been explained.
The remainder is similar to this; this is the meaning of a "pseudo-example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
What is meant by "the remainder"?

It refers to cases where, regarding the thesis (*sādhya*), the proof (*sādhana*), and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), although there is a combination or separation [of these elements], they are stated in a perverted manner.

Alternatively, in this case, there is no application or exclusion; rather, only the presence of both the *sādhya* (the probandum) and the *sādhana* (the probans) in the subject (*pakṣa*) is established, while both are absent in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
Regarding these two properties, it may be that one or the other is unestablished or not excluded, or it may be that both are unestablished or not excluded.
For example, one might establish the thesis: "Sound is eternal because it lacks tangibility.
As a corroborative instance based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one might state: "Whatever lacks tangibility is seen to be eternal, such as karma, atoms (*paramāṇu*), or a jar," and so forth.

Regarding the statement of a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), it refers to such claims as: "All impermanent things are observed to possess tangibility, like atoms, like karma, or like space," and so forth.

By this, it has already been explained that there is a failure to establish the subject (*dharmin*) within the dissimilar example, namely, when one opposes those who do not accept that space and the like are permanent.
Must both types of analogical statements be fully provided for them to constitute a valid proof (*sādhana*), or may it suffice to state only one, as is done with the reason (*hetu*)?

According to correct reasoning, both should be stated; for by providing both, one fully demonstrates that the probandum (*sādhya*) is not separate from its reason, thereby fully showing its necessary presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its universal absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), which correctly counteracts the fallacies of contradiction (*viruddha*) and uncertainty (*anaikāntika*).
If one part [of the reason] is already established for [the opponent], then stating even that one part constitutes a valid proof (*sādhana*).
If, as in the case of the word "sound," both meanings are already accepted by both parties, there is no need to state either of them.
Alternatively, by implication of the meaning, one [mark] can manifest two [conclusions].
Furthermore, this principle is seen only within inference (*anumāna*):

if this characteristic is ascertained at the object of inference, one recalls its definite presence in other similar instances and its universal absence in those where it is absent; thus, from this, a definitive understanding arises.
Therefore, the root verse says:
Just as one has reached certainty for oneself, One desires that certainty arise in others;
Thus, the thesis, the reason, and the example Are taught, while all else is excluded.
The statement of the reason (*hetu*) is made to reveal the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) within that which is to be inferred;
the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is made to reveal the inseparable relationship (*avinābhāva*) therein;
and the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is made to reveal that which is to be inferred.
Within the object of inference (*anumeya*), there are no other members besides these; by this, other investigations (*parīkṣā*) and so forth, as well as the *saṃyoga* and *nigamana*, are excluded.
If that is the case, then the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should not be a separate member, because it serves to manifest the meaning of the reason (*hetu*).

Although this is indeed the case, these words regarding the "reason" (hetu) serve solely to clarify that it is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma), and not to clarify the presence or absence [of the reason] in similar instances (sapakṣa) or dissimilar instances (vipakṣa); therefore, one must separately state the examples of similarity and dissimilarity.
If the meaning expressed by the words "only the reason" (*hetu*) is what is called the "reason," what fault would there be?
And what merit would there be?
To speak of the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) as a separate member constitutes its merit.
This should be understood as being like the worldly expedient expressions [of "producedness"], which are entirely inconsistent with the meaning of the actual cause.
If this were so, what would be the fault?

This statement merely serves as an analogy for the established thesis (*sādhya*), which lacks functional efficacy and is not the actual probans (*sādhana*), because it merely states the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which is the common property (*sādharmya*) shared with the example.
It does not state the meaning of the probans (*sādhana*) or the probandum (*sādhya*).

Furthermore, because the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are distinct, this [reason] possesses both the similar instance (*sādharmya*) and the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*), yet it ultimately cannot demonstrate the inseparability (*avinābhāvitva*) between the reason and the probandum. Therefore, while it merely resembles the meaning of the probandum, it lacks functional efficacy.
Why is it incapable? Because within a homologous example (*sapakṣa*), the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣārtha*) do not necessarily correspond;
furthermore, since this [example] would itself have to be established by another illustration, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that there are various categories [of examples]; nor can something from a different category—which does not manifest the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and lacks the capacity for specific distinction—serve as an analogy.
Therefore, a verse says:
"If the reason is merely the thesis itself, Or if it belongs to a different class of characteristics,"
The analogies would be endless, as would the refutations of dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

In the world, however, an example of a different property (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) merely demonstrates that the reason (*hetu*) exists in a location other than the thesis (*pakṣa*), namely in a dissimilar instance; it does not possess the power [to prove the conclusion] because it is not the case that the reason is necessarily absent wherever the thesis is absent.
If the property of the subject alone were the nature of the reason (*hetu*), then even that which is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) would necessarily become a valid reason.

How could such a fallacy occur when both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), as well as the two types of examples—the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—are fully present?

If at that time the established dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) were not of a single type, this fault would indeed arise; however, as in the case of the final examples for each of the first and last [reasons], the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) are established solely to reveal the logical reason (*hetu*).
By this principle, although every part is capable of serving as a reason to manifest what is to be established (*sādhya*), only one part is stated for the time being as the reason.

Thus, the brief exposition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, along with their fallacies, constitutes what is called the "proof" (*sādhana*) and the "fallacious proof" (*sādhanābhāsa*). These multiple statements are designated by those names.
According to what is appropriate, these means of proof (*sādhana*) and fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) are taught for the sake of enlightening others.

For one's own enlightenment, there are only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); since terms such as "sound" and "example" are subsumed within these, there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because it is through these that one can comprehend both specific (svalakṣaṇa) and general (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) characteristics, there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) distinct from these two for which another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be established.
Therefore, the root verse says:
"Direct perception is free from conceptual construction; The others are said to arise from causes."

Regarding the phrase "direct perception is free from conceptual construction" (*pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍham*): if a cognition, with respect to objects such as form (*rūpa*), is devoid of all types of conceptualization—including those based on names, designations, conventions, non-differentiation, and various categories—and functions individually and directly toward its unique object, it is therefore called direct perception.
Therefore, it is said in verse:
The dharmas do not have a single characteristic; The faculties do not encompass all modes of activity.
Only through internal realization and beyond words Is the realm of the material faculties known.
The mental level (*manobhūmi*) also includes states that are free from all conceptualization and proceed solely as direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).

Furthermore, the self-cognizing portions (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of craving and other such states, as well as the states of those practicing meditative concentration who are free from conceptualization based on scripture, are all direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, within this context, there is no separate result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), because this very entity arises as if it were an object and appears as if it had utility; thus, it is conventionally designated as "valid cognition.
If the self-reflexive portions (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*) of craving and so forth are also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), why is conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) excluded from this category?
This does not preclude the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) within this [consciousness], for it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
However, when one apprehends an object other than itself within this [consciousness], it is not termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For this reason, it is said that recollection, inference, desire, doubtful cognition, deluded cognition, and so forth, are all not direct perceptions with respect to coarse objects and the like, because they arise as conceptualizations following what was previously experienced.

Thus, within all conventional existence, cognitions such as those of a jar, number, lifting, existence, and the nature of a jar appear to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, they operate by constructing other mental images regarding truly existent objects and by turning toward conceptualizations that falsely conjoin other meanings.
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has already been explained; inference (*anumāna*) shall now be discussed.

Regarding the phrase "arising from other stated reasons": this means that cognition is the subsequent cognition arising from other probative reasons as previously described, and it takes that object as its referent.
This is of two kinds:
first, the wisdom that scrutinizes the object of inference, which arises from either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*);

and second, the recollection that this reason (*hetu*) is inseparable from the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established. By means of this, the force of what was previously stated is accomplished, because one recollects that the reason is necessarily present in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and so forth.
Because these serve as the grounds for inference based on what is proximate and remote, both are termed "inference" (*anumāna*); this is stated in terms of the instrument and the agent.
One should understand that inference for the sake of convincing others (*parārthānumāna*) is likewise established as a means of proof (*sādhana*) without departing from these [grounds].
Therefore, it is said in verse:
A single entity possesses many properties, Yet its characteristics do not function as all [of them] simultaneously;
It is only by way of excluding the others That it expresses a specific determination which can follow along.
Thus, these characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also manifold dharmas;
they do not transcend that which is characterized (*lakṣya*), for it is they alone that can indicate it, and nothing else.
Why, then, is this established as distinct from the previously mentioned direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

Two gates are presented here; in this context, it should also be stated that inference regarding an effect is "inference" (anumāna), and in that context, it should also be stated that direct perception regarding a cause is "direct perception" (pratyakṣa), as neither is precluded.
The means of proof (*sādhana*) and the fallacies of the means of proof have already been explained; now the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) and the fallacies of refutation shall be explained.
The verse says:
"Refutation consists of the statement of deficiencies and so forth; the fallacies of refutation are said to be of various kinds."

Regarding the phrase "the refutations consisting of the deficiency of terms, etc. herein: this refers to the faults of the constituent parts, such as the deficiency of words and so forth, mentioned previously.
Each of those individual terms is called a "refutation" because each one individually serves to demonstrate that the preceding thesis is not well-stated.

Regarding the statement, "What are called 'pseudo-refutations' are various fallacies," this means that similar fallacies such as the *sādharmya-sama* (balancing the homogeneity) and so forth are termed "pseudo-refutations" because they are for the most part established by others to mislead them regarding sound inference (*saddharmānumāna*).
Because it fails to demonstrate the faults of the opponent’s position— since it refutes them through irrational means— and because it merely establishes its own position,
it is called a "pseudo-fallacy" (jāti) as it belongs to that same class.

If one establishes such a designation within an irrational inference, or fails to recognize the fault of that inference, or does so merely to reveal the door to its faults, it is not termed a "pseudo-fault" (*jāti*).
Because it demonstrates a different category:
by establishing similarity through shared properties (*sādharmya*), there is similarity;
otherwise, it is by means of dissimilar properties (*vaidharmya*).
To distinguish and differentiate is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*);
it should be one and without difference.
To manifest other reasons for what has been established is called "similarity of obtainability" (*upalabdhisama*).
Because it is difficult to distinguish the meaning and is the cause of doubt, it is called "hesitation" (*vimarśa*).
Because it expresses a different category (*vipakṣa*), it is undesirable; the meaning of the term follows accordingly.

Herein, regarding the phrase "because it demonstrates a different category, it is established through a different property, being similar to the same property": it is called "established through difference" because it establishes [the thesis] in a reversed manner. This is stated in terms of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).

"Similarity of the same property" (*sādharmya-samā*) means that it is similar to the same property; thus it is called "similarity of the same property. This is because it is a fallacy of similarity included within all [types of] established [fallacies].
The term "similarity" (*samā*) is in the neuter gender because it functions as a refutation of the corresponding [argument], or because it follows the requirements of the verse meter.
What is the refutation by means of similarity through shared properties?
It is stated thus because the agent is spoken of in relation to the action, and because [the action] arises through transformation;
subsequent instances should also be explained accordingly.
Now, in this context, because the proof is established through an inverted application of the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), it is called "resemblance by similarity" (*sādharmya-sama*).
For example, when one establishes: "Sound is impermanent, because it is produced by volitional effort," and uses space (*ākāśa*) as the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
There is a case where space (*ākāśa*) is cited as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), on the grounds that it lacks material form and so forth, in order to establish that "sound is eternal.

In this manner, while the pot (*ghaṭa*)—which is actually part of the same category as the subject (*pakṣa*) in the stated reason—should be the similar instance, space, which belongs to a different category (*vipakṣa*), is instead presented as the similar instance. This is therefore called "similarity to the similar instance" (*sādharmya-sama*).

Regarding the phrase "the other by dissimilar properties" (*vaidharmya-sama*): this means that similarity based on dissimilar properties is the counterpart to the previously mentioned similarity based on similar properties (*sādharmya-sama*).

It demonstrates a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) established through an inverted dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Among the two types of examples, as established previously, a jar is posited as the dissimilar instance; therefore, it is called similarity based on dissimilar properties.

Regarding the statement, "Discriminating distinctions is discrimination": because the previous [section] demonstrated [the general nature of] manifestation and so forth, whereas the present [section] explains the discrimination of distinctions, one should understand that discrimination refers to the distinctions among phenomena of the same kind.

That is to say, as previously stated, the jar is taken as the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*); since within that similar instance there exists the distinct property of being combustible and so forth, it follows that the jar must be impermanent, whereas sound is not [combustible], and thus sound must be permanent.

Because there are distinctions such as "incapable of being burned" and so forth, this [position] is established through conceptualization and inversion; therefore, it is called "resemblance to conceptualization.

As for the statement, "It would follow that they become one and there is no difference," this demonstrates that the same fault has already been stated previously, because by virtue of this, they would necessarily become one with that.
Who is that person?
Because no other expedient means is heard of thereafter and because they are situated in immediate proximity, one should know that this refers to the [opponent's] own thesis.
"Establishing non-difference" means establishing the fallacy of non-difference.
Since the meaning can be understood from these very words, there is no need to state whose names they are or with whom they are shared to establish their non-difference.
Because they are not specified individually, it refers to "all of this" being identical to "all of that."

As it has been said: "If, because a jar or other such things share a common property (*sādharmya*), it were to follow that all other properties are likewise without distinction, then all properties of a jar would necessarily exist in sound; consequently, all things, being identical in their mutual properties, would become a single nature."

In this context, suppressing [the distinction] would result in the fault of non-differentiation; furthermore, it is intended to demonstrate the difference between the word "vase" and [its referent]. Since this is not significantly different from the previous analysis of similarity, it should be explained separately.

If one establishes "impermanence" by means of "that which is produced through uninterrupted effort," intending to show that both are non-eternal natures, then the fallacy of the thesis and the reason being indistinguishable occurs.
Furthermore, because this causes [the subject] to be established as having no distinct nature, it is called "non-different similarity" (*aviśeṣasama*).
Some say that this reason, just as it can establish the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), can also establish a property contrary to it.
Because there is no distinction, it is therefore called "similarity through non-difference" (*aviśeṣasama*).

Regarding "manifesting another reason for the thesis being established, which is called 'similarity through obtainability' (*upalabdhisama*)," this means that if one demonstrates that another reason for the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) can be obtained, it is then called "similarity through obtainability."
That is to say, some may argue:

"The previous proof that 'sound is impermanent' is not a valid reason, because impermanence can be established through other reasons—such as direct perception—in the case of lightning, light, and so forth."
If that [effect] could exist apart from this [cause], then this would not be the cause of that.
Others have proposed a different argument here, claiming that this is not the correct primary cause for the impermanence of that, because it is not pervasive.
As it is said: "The forest possesses deliberation, because it possesses sleep.

Regarding the statement, "Because it is difficult to distinguish the meaning from doubt, it is called 'hesitation' (vimarśa)," it is expressed in the feminine gender because it corresponds to a category of logical fallacy (*hetvābhāsa*).
In this context, when one analyzes the difference in the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason becomes inconclusive; therefore, it is called "resemblance to doubt" (*saṃśayasama*).
Alternatively, when one analyzes the difference in the meaning of the reason (*hetu*), it is likewise termed the fallacy of "resemblance to doubt."
That is to say, some might argue:
"As previously established, 'sound is impermanent because it is produced by effort without interval.
Since we observe that what is produced by effort without interval is either manifested or generated, doubt arises."
Is that which is now established intended to manifest [the meaning] or to produce it?
Therefore, one should not use such a reason to prove the meaning of impermanence.
Regarding the statement, "Because it explains the meaning of a dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), it is undesirable; the name and its meaning follow accordingly":
That is to say, some may argue:

"If that which is produced by diligent effort without interval is said to be impermanent, then by logical implication, all things such as lightning and light—which are not produced by diligent effort without interval—should necessarily be permanent."
This is called "similarity by implication" (*arthāpatti-sama*).
One should know that in this context, the latter part of the phrase has been omitted; therefore, it is simply termed "hesitation" (*vimarśa*) and "implication.
Furthermore, for what reason does this "similarity by parity of reasoning" (*tulyadharmatva-sama*) differ from the sequence taught by other masters of Hetuvidyā?

Because it is similar to [the fallacy of] "contradicting the same" (*sādharmya-sama*). For this reason, because there are many such doubts regarding the "same property" (*sādharmya*) and so forth, they are "similar" (*pratibimba*) to that [fallacy].
The word "many" (*bahu*) is used to indicate that there may be other objections, and to indicate the fallacies of "pseudo-unestablished reasons" (*asiddha-hetu*).

Among these, the first four do not correspond at all with the skillful means of the metaphors I have taught; however, following worldly conventions of metaphorical skillful means, although they do not explicitly reveal that the cause is of a determinate nature, they nevertheless encompass its essence, and thus this statement was made.

By employing reasons such as "indefinite due to lack of application" (*anaikāntika-sādhāraṇa*) to establish one's own position, while provisionally asserting that the opponent likewise possesses this property, it consequently becomes a fallacy of the "pseudo-common indefinite" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika-pratibimba*), or alternatively, it becomes a "pseudo-contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin-pratibimba*).
If it is said that [the reason] is intended solely to establish one's own position, how can it be called a "refutation" (dūṣaṇa) when it is inconclusive?
It is not that this very [inconclusive reason] is called a refutation; rather, it is called "inconclusive" because it presents a difficulty regarding the claim of inconclusiveness.
Since the signified is spoken of within the signifier, this fault does not arise.
Other cases should likewise be established in this manner.

If the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) one has established suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), or if the reason—such as "being of the same nature" (*tulyatva*)—is definitively established for the opponent, then that itself is called a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
Because these [reasons] are difficult to refute, if one relies on the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*) cannot negate their nature.

For example, if someone were to establish that "sound is not audible, like a jar," this would be refuted by the fact that sound is directly perceived as being audible; yet one should not use its audibility to negate its impermanence, for it is not the case that mere non-perception can constitute a negation.
If it were otherwise, then permanence too would have to be negated.
The second type, "non-different similarity" (*aviśeṣasama*), is the fallacy of a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*) consisting of non-establishment (*asiddha*).

This is because it superimposes [existence] upon that which was originally non-existent to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*), thereby committing the fallacy of making the reason (*hetu*) identical to the thesis.
This uses the principle that what was originally non-existent can arise as an ultimate cause to prove non-existence after cessation.
If one were to establish that very point [as the probandum], it could serve as a refutation.

The third [type of] "similar" fallacy consists of establishing a contradiction that harms the thesis; it is considered a pseudo-refutation because it is inconclusive, as in the case of [the argument regarding] combustibility and so forth.
If it were determinate, it would constitute a contradiction.
Since one can find a similar instance that renders the thesis indeterminate, it constitutes a fallacy;
if the reason adduced for the thesis also exists in the case of permanence, it can constitute a valid refutation.

Secondly, although "perceptibility" (*upalabdhi*) is not all-pervasive (*avyāpin*), it does not constitute the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*) because there are no other instances [of the subject] where it is absent;
if the probandum (*sādhya*) were absent, it could indeed be called a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). However, it is not intended here to establish that everything is impermanent (*anitya*).

The "resemblance to doubt" (*saṃśayasama*) refers to the following: if one seeks to establish destruction through the uninterrupted exertion of effort, yet attempts to render the probandum inconclusive by superimposing "arising" onto it, this is a fallacy resembling the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

If, however, one does not engage in such conceptual differentiation regarding the probandum, but merely raises an objection by distinguishing the arising of the reason itself, this is a fallacy resembling the unestablished (*asiddha*).

In this context, one does not intend to establish only the arising [of a thing] as its destruction; rather, whether it be arising or manifestation, both are subject to destruction, for they are not indeterminate.
By extension, the meaning is similar: because the objection is raised on the grounds of being "indeterminate" (*anaikāntika*) due to perversion, it is a "pseudo-indeterminate" (*anaikāntika-ābhāsa*).

If one were to establish "permanent" and "impermanent" based on whether or not something is produced by uninterrupted effort, or if one were to claim that only what is produced by uninterrupted effort is impermanent while nothing else is, then these positions could be subject to refutation.
Whether the cause reaches [the object] or does not reach it, in all three times, [the reason] is an unpalatable statement;
whether it reaches or does not reach, it lacks a cause. This is called the fallacy of a deficient reason (hetv-ābhāsa).

Regarding the statement, "If the reason reaches or does not reach [the thesis], it is an unpalatable [position] in all three times; reaching or not reaching constitutes no reason," this expresses an unpalatable critique of both reaching and not reaching:

if the reason could establish the thesis by reaching it, then because there would be no distinction, it would not be the thesis to be established—just as the waters of a pond and the sea, when merged, are indistinguishable.
Furthermore, if [the probandum] is not established, it should not be reached by the mark (*liṅga*);
if what is to be established were established, what would be the reason for this?

If the establishing reason does not reach the thing to be established, then because there would be no distinction between "not reaching" and "not being a reason," it should fail to function as a reason.
This is called the "similarity of reaching and not reaching.
Furthermore, one may raise an objection regarding the three times:
if the reason (*hetu*) is established prior to that which is to be established (*sādhya*), then since the *sādhya* does not yet exist, of what would this be the reason?
If you say [the cause] comes later, then that which is to be established is already accomplished; what further need is there for a cause?
If they exist simultaneously, then neither the cause nor the possessor of the cause is established, like the two horns of a cow.
This is called the "fallacy of the semblance of no cause" (*ahetv-ābhāsa*).
In this context, the difference from the previous sequence is that both are stated to lack a semblance of a reason (*hetv-ābhāsa*). Why is this so?
This is because it irrationaly denies all causes.
What is the reasoning here?
It is simply that they do not reach the same [effect]; therefore, even if they possess the characteristics of a cause, they are not called causes.
What is the reasoning for this?
Because it cannot be designated as a "reason" (hetu) prior to that which is to be established (sādhya), it is not a "means of establishment" (sādhana).
Furthermore, in this case, there is the fallacy of self-defeat (svaviruddha), because it negates its own [status as a] similar instance (sapakṣa).

Thus, while there is an "apparent reason" (*hetvābhāsa*) lacking [the necessary members] among those established by words and wisdom, there is an "apparent unestablishedness" (*asiddha*) among reasons regarding the actual meaning, because they irrationally deny the causes of all phenomena.
As with the two preceding reasons, since that which is established in meaning is neither the produced nor the producer, it does not accord with correct reasoning;
if one refutes it by means of correct reasoning, it may be called a valid refutation.
Because it is stated that there is no prior cause, there should be nothing established;
this is called "resemblance to non-statement.
The same applies to arising and non-arising.
When the probans is dissimilar in even a slight degree, it reveals that the thesis is unestablished;
this is called the "fallacy of the similar-to-the-probandum" (*kāryasama*). It is for the most part like the [fallacy] of the similar-to-the-thesis (*pratijñāsama*).
Regarding the statement, "Because the previously stated reason does not exist, that which is to be established should also not exist; this is called 'resemblance to non-statement' (avācyasama)":
it means that some say, "If, as previously established, impermanence is proven by this reason, then prior to its being stated, [the reason] did not exist at all;
since the reason does not exist, [the subject] should not be impermanent."
This is called the "semblance of non-explanation" (*avāda-samā*).

Regarding the phrase "the same applies to arising and non-arising": since there is no cause prior to arising, there is nothing established; this is likewise termed the "semblance of non-arising" (*anutpāda-samā*).
Regarding the statement "it is likewise," because the reason [adduced] prior to the sound lacks any basis for its application, there should be no thesis to be established.
One should understand that just as there is no thesis established here, there is likewise a contradiction with what is to be established.
That is to say, some may argue:
"According to what was previously established, if such a sound did not exist prior to its production through effort and uninterrupted exertion, it would not be impermanent;
furthermore, since it is not produced through effort and uninterrupted exertion, it must therefore be permanent."
This is called the "fallacy of similarity through non-arising" (*anutpatti-sama*).
Regarding the statement, "The 'fallacy of similarity through the partial difference of the effect' (*kārya-sama*) reveals that the probandum is unestablished":

this refers to the case where one seeks to establish that "sound is impermanent because it is a product, like a jar. If it is the jar that is impermanent due to its being a product, what relevance does that have to the matter of sound?
This is called "similarity of the probandum" (*kāryasama*).

Regarding the phrase "mostly like the statement of the thesis," this refers to various forms of "similarity of the unestablished" (*asiddhasama*) and so forth that mostly resemble the statement of the point to be established; for example, it is like the fallacy of an unestablished reason (*asiddhahetu*).
The word "many" (bahu) is used to indicate that [the fallacy] may resemble other types.

In this context, there is no mention of a "resemblance to a superimposed inference" (*sādhyasama-upacāra-anumāna*), which refers to establishing impermanence in the words spoken by a proponent on the grounds that the reason does not exist prior to its being stated; this is a semblance of "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Alternatively, it is a semblance of "lack of a reason" (*hetv-nyūna*), because the capacity to establish the proof (*sādhana*) does not exist prior to its being stated.

If, within this context, the meaning being expressed is non-existent, and if at the time of establishing the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) there is no verbal expression, one may constitute a valid refutation.

Regarding "resemblance to non-arising" (*anutpatti-sama*): if one superimposes the probandum (*sādhya*) before the sound has even arisen, and then objects that the reason (*hetu*) is absent, this is called a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).
However, if at the time of establishing [the argument] one demonstrates that this [reason] is non-existent, one may constitute a valid refutation.

If, prior to its production, one attempts to prove that sound is permanent by challenging it with the reason "not produced through immediate volitional effort," this argument is also seemingly inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it applies by way of partial exclusion (*vyatireka*).
There are three types of similarity regarding what is produced (*kṛtaka*):
if one challenges the presence of the property of being produced in a jar and so forth by claiming it does not exist in sound, this is a fallacy of "seeming non-establishment" (*asiddha-sābhāsa*).
If one objects that "producedness" (kṛtakatva) does not exist in jars and the like [as a property of sound], this is a pseudo-contradiction (viruddhābhāsa);
if one objects that it likewise does not exist in the subject itself as being eternal, this is a pseudo-indeterminate (anaikāntikābhāsa) because it is an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reason.
Alternatively, this may be considered a fallacy of analogy, because it cites a similar instance. Why is this?
It is because inference is established by apprehending only the general property (*sāmānyadharma*), and not the particular.
If one were to grasp a distinct meaning based on a definitive difference, inference would be impossible.
To seek a reason for what is already mutually accepted is called the "fallacy of the similar-to-the-produced" (*utpādasama*).
To raise an objection regarding the example is called the "pseudo-example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
Regarding the statement, "When both [parties] accept [the thesis] yet seek a reason, it is called the 'fallacy of similarity to production' (utpattisama)':
this refers to an objection stating, 'As for the previously established [thesis] that "jars and so forth are impermanent," by what reason is this further proven?'"

Regarding the statement, "This is a refutation based on an analogy, termed a 'pseudo-analogy' (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa)," it means that since both parties agree that things such as jars are established as impermanent, to raise a refutation claiming they are not so established constitutes a pseudo-analogy; therefore, it is called a "pseudo-analogy."
"Because impermanence always follows it, it is called 'resembling permanence.
This constitutes the fallacy of establishing permanence; it is termed a 'fallacy similar to the thesis' (*pakṣasama*).
To explain, there is an objection as follows:"

Regarding the previously established proposition that "sound is impermanent," this [sound] should be conjoined with both permanence and impermanence, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is never abandoned; thus, it should also be permanent.
This is called the fallacy of "resemblance to permanence" (*nitya-sama*).
It is a fallacy of the thesis because it superimposes a permanence upon that which is to be established—impermanence.

In this context, there is no separate, real impermanence upon which permanence could depend; rather, it is this very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) itself that is termed "impermanent" because it was previously non-existent and now exists, and having existed for a time, it returns to non-existence.
This very state, by virtue of its own nature and conditions, is termed "impermanence," just as [the term] "fruit-ness" [is applied to a fruit].
Such fallacies are for the most part what Caraka stated; they are generally described as having the nature of a "pseudo-refutation" (dūṣaṇābhāsa) because they are so well-established.
The explanations provided in other treatises should likewise be established through such distinctions.
These very same types of fallacies, though established as infinite varieties due to slight differences in their specific applications, are not mentioned here.

In this regard, whatever has been stated concerning superimposition (*samāropa*), denial (*apavāda*), manifestation (*prakāśa*), non-manifestation (*aprakāśa*), the principle of production (*utpatti-nīti*), distinct analogies (*bhinnopamā*), and similarity of categories (*jāti-sādṛśya*), all of these should be scrutinized and refuted according to this same methodological approach.

Various unwholesome proponents of inference employ such methods of exposition that they proliferate and ramify indefinitely; since these are explained exhaustively in other treatises, I shall not discuss them further here.

Furthermore, regarding the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), whatever was previously stated by the masters of logic (*hetuvidyā*) has been omitted here: some fall within the category of "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*), some are excessively crude, and some are irrational, resembling types of deceptive speech. Therefore, they have not been recorded.
All the categories and meanings asserted by other masters should likewise be analyzed and established in this manner.

Such [assertions] as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and so forth are all unreasonable, as they contradict the characteristics already explained; they are all termed "ignorance" because they are extremely remote from the truth.
Furthermore, regarding these types of fallacious arguments, I have already largely refuted them within my own works, such as the *Nyāyamukha* and others.
Moreover, I have already analyzed this point in detail in my critique of the ancient *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*; therefore, let us now desist.
To open for the wise the poison-removing medicine of wisdom, And to unlock this gateway of sublime meaning and correct principle,
I cause those who are deluded by external measures To transcend the deviant paths and realize the true meaning.
The Root Treatise on the Gateway to Logic (Nyāyamukha-śāstra)
